 # Windows Internet Name Service (WINS) | Microsoft Learn
 
-Windows Internet Name Service (WINS) is a legacy computer name registration and resolution service that maps computer NetBIOS names to IP addresses.
+Windows Internet Name Service (WINS) is a legacy service that maps Network Basic Input/Output System (NetBIOS) computer names to Internet Protocol (IP) addresses. Microsoft plans to remove WINS. If your organization still uses it, plan a transition.
+
+This article explains WINS availability and removal plans and provides guidance for migrating name resolution to Domain Name System (DNS).
+
+## WINS availability in Windows Server 2025 and planned removal in Windows Server 2028
+
+WINS is available in Windows Server 2025, the final Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) release to include and support it. Microsoft continues to support WINS as part of Windows Server 2025 throughout the [Windows Server 2025 lifecycle](/en-us/lifecycle/products/windows-server-2025).
+
+WINS has been removed in Windows Server 2028 Preview. To learn more, see the [Windows Server 2028 Preview removal notice](../../../get-started/removed-deprecated-features-windows-server?tabs=ws28-preview#features-removed). For removal details, see [WINS removal: Moving forward with modern name resolution](https://support.microsoft.com/servicing/os/windows/docs/2025/11/wins-removal-moving-forward-with-modern-name-resolution).
 
-If you do not already have WINS deployed on your network, do not deploy WINS - instead, deploy Domain Name System (DNS). DNS also provides computer name registration and resolution services, and includes many additional benefits over WINS, such as integration with Active Directory Domain Services.
+If your network doesn't already have a WINS deployment, don't deploy WINS. Instead, deploy Domain Name System (DNS). DNS also provides computer name registration and resolution services, and includes many additional benefits over WINS, such as integration with Active Directory Domain Services.
 
 For more information, see [Domain Name System (DNS)](../../dns/dns-top)
 
-If you have already deployed WINS on your network, it is recommended that you deploy DNS and then decommission WINS.
\ No newline at end of file
+If your network already has a WINS deployment, we recommend deploying DNS and then decommissioning WINS.
\ No newline at end of file

englishSummary.headline: WINS removal is planned for Windows Server 2028
englishSummary.summary: The documentation states that WINS remains supported throughout the Windows Server 2025 lifecycle but has been removed from Windows Server 2028 Preview. It adds guidance for replacing WINS with DNS.
englishSummary.adminImpact: Organizations using WINS should plan a transition to DNS and decommission WINS.

-# SMBv1 Not Installed by Default in Windows Server and Windows | Microsoft Learn
+# SMBv1 Availability: Windows Server and Windows | Microsoft Learn
 
-The Server Message Block version 1 (SMBv1) protocol is deprecated and no longer installed by default in modern versions of Windows and Windows Server. This article provides an overview of SMBv1's removal, its behavior in various Windows editions, and alternatives for legacy compatibility. Learn how to address issues related to SMBv1, explore best practices, and understand the implications of its absence in network environments.
+Server Message Block version 1 (SMBv1) is a legacy network file-sharing protocol that Windows uses to access shared files and printers. Because SMBv1 has significant security vulnerabilities, Windows 11 and Windows Server 2019 through Windows Server 2025 don't install it by default. Starting with Windows Server 2028 Preview, Windows Server no longer includes SMBv1, and you can't install or enable it. For more information, see [SMBv1 removal in Windows Server 2028](../../../get-started/removed-deprecated-features-windows-server#features-removed).
 
-## Default behavior for SMBv1
+This article explains SMBv1 behavior for these Windows releases and provides alternatives for legacy compatibility.
+
+## Default behavior for SMBv1 in Windows Server 2028 Preview and earlier releases
 
 Since Windows 10, version 1709 and Windows Server, version 1709, the Server Message Block version 1 (SMBv1) network protocol is no longer installed by default. SMBv2 and later protocols superseded SMBv1 starting in 2007. Microsoft publicly deprecated the SMBv1 protocol in 2014.
 
-SMBv1 has the following behavior in Windows 10 and Windows Server 2019 and later versions:
+Important
+
+Starting with Windows Server 2028 Preview, Windows Server no longer includes SMBv1. For more information, see [SMBv1 removal in Windows Server 2028](../../../get-started/removed-deprecated-features-windows-server#features-removed). You can't install or enable SMBv1 on Windows Server 2028 Preview. Guidance in this article for reinstalling or re-enabling SMBv1 applies only to earlier Windows Server versions and Windows client versions where SMBv1 remains available as an optional component.
+
+SMBv1 has the following installation and removal behavior across affected Windows client and Windows Server releases:
 
 - SMBv1 now has both client and server sub-features that can be uninstalled separately.
 - Windows 10 Enterprise, Windows 10 Education, and Windows 10 Pro for Workstations no longer contain the SMBv1 client or server by default after a clean installation.
-- Windows Server 2019 and later no longer contains the SMBv1 client or server by default after a clean installation.
+- Windows Server 2019 through Windows Server 2025 don't contain the SMBv1 client or server by default after a clean installation.
 - Windows 10 Home and Windows 10 Pro no longer contain the SMBv1 server by default after a clean installation.
 - Windows 11 doesn't contain the SMBv1 server or client by default after a clean installation.
 - Windows 10 Home and Windows 10 Pro, version 1709 still contain the SMBv1 client by default after a clean installation. If the SMBv1 client isn't used for 15 days in total (excluding the computer being turned off), it automatically uninstalls itself. Starting in Windows 10, version 1809, Windows 10 Pro no longer contains the SMBv1 client by default after a clean installation.

englishSummary.headline: SMBv1 is removed from Windows Server 2028 Preview
englishSummary.summary: The documentation now states that Windows Server 2028 Preview no longer includes SMBv1 and cannot install or enable it. Windows Server 2019–2025 still omit SMBv1 by default.
englishSummary.adminImpact: Audit SMBv1 usage and update or replace dependent systems before upgrading to Windows Server 2028 Preview.

 ### Use UEFI firmware
 
-- Secure Boot or UEFI firmware isn't required on the physical Hyper-V host. For generation 2 VMs, Hyper-V provides virtual firmware to virtual machines that is independent of what's on the Hyper-V host.
+- Physical Hyper-V hosts that run Windows Server 2025 or earlier don't require Secure Boot or UEFI firmware. For generation 2 VMs, Hyper-V provides virtual firmware that is independent of the physical Hyper-V host's firmware.
 - UEFI firmware in a generation 2 virtual machine doesn't support setup mode for Secure Boot.
